doc.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Leading the band on the Arthur Godfrey Show
summary: Hyman conducted Godfrey's three-keyboard band, which turned to jazz and played hip material, later taping shows.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: Some of our younger viewers might not remember the Arthur Godfrey Show, but did you have some experiences in there that were new? It must have been that every week something would come along.

It was a daily show and additional — a daily radio show — and additional occasional television shows. Well I really was in a position to be forced to learn very quickly quite a number of things. I had to make sure my conducting was up to standards, because many of those things were not just beating off tempo, they were conducting music comedy or even light opera kind of material. And it was a peculiar band. I acquired the band you might say, and it already included Lee Irwin on organ, and Lud Flato on piano. So we turned it into a three keyboard band. I played perhaps more Hammond organ than piano in that show. The fellow who had been there, Lee Irwin, he played Allen organ and we divided up the functions. And Flato, on piano, was very useful playing a Trylvestan keyboard glockenspiel if I was busy doing something else. So that worked out fine.
Were you responsible for sound effects, anything like that?

No we didn’t do that. No the strange thing about that show was that Godfrey had fallen in love with jazz. And we turned it into a jazz band. Sometimes it was a Dixieland band and Godfrey would play along with his ukulele, and he was very cooperative in wanting to learn the correct chords. And at other times he would give us free reign and we did everything from Charlie Mingus to whatever was happening back then, back then being 1959, 1960. We played amazingly hip things for the Arthur Godfrey Show. “Bags’ Groove,” Charlie Mingus, “This Here, Dat Dere,” Bobby Timmons, things like that. We got away with murder, frankly. Everybody seemed to like it.
And it was live too, right?
Not always. After a while we would tape, then we’d tape maybe two shows a day and then have the rest of the week off, that kind of thing.
